Neural retrieval with embeddings: when dense vectors win

Embeddings map a passage and a query into the same vector space. Retrieval becomes nearest-neighbour search over that space, which lets a query phrased in different words still find the passage that answers it.

Dense vectors are excellent for conceptual questions. Ask for "how do I stop a background job from running twice" and a good bi-encoder will retrieve a page about idempotency keys that never uses the word job.

The cost side

Every embedding model is a fixed cost: disk for the weights, memory for the encoder, and time proportional to the corpus size when you index. Approximate nearest neighbour structures such as HNSW add their own memory and their own recall curve to tune.

For a desktop application that must work on a plane, the honest tradeoff is a small local encoder or none at all. A hosted embedding endpoint turns an offline feature into a network dependency.

Failure modes

Dense retrieval is weak on long numbers, rare product names and exact code identifiers, because those tokens are underrepresented in training data. Hybrid retrieval exists precisely because the two failure modes are opposites.
